title: Watson Lecture: Katie Bouman Discusses Imaging the Invisible
author: Caltech Media Relations (mr@caltech.edu)
summary: How can we extend the limits of observation to “see” the seemingly invisible? On Wednesday, November 4, 2026, Katie Bouman, professor of computing and mathematical sciences, electrical engineering and astronomy; Rosenberg Scholar; and a Heritage Medical Research Institute Investigator, will share how her lab combines physics and machine learning to see things in the universe that are invisible to traditional sensors.
text:
How can we extend the limits of observation to "see" the seemingly invisible? On Wednesday, November 4, 2026, Katie Bouman, professor of computing and mathematical sciences, electrical engineering and astronomy; Rosenberg Scholar; and a Heritage Medical Research Institute Investigator, will share how her lab combines physics and machine learning to see things in the universe that are invisible to traditional sensors.
In a public talk titled "Illuminating the Hidden Universe with Physics and AI," Bouman will explain how scientific images are increasingly constructed rather than simply captured, not only in extreme astrophysics—such as through black hole imaging—but also in other disciplines.
For centuries, traditional cameras and photography have been modeled on the human eye, Bouman explains. "But if we want to see things that traditional cameras can't, we need to rethink what a camera can be. Instead of simply trying to capture what our eyes would see, we can design sensors that collect information in entirely new ways, then use algorithms and machine learning to fill in missing pieces. The key is doing this responsibly, making sure that what we reconstruct is still grounded in the physics of the measurements we actually collect."
Growing up in West Lafayette, Indiana, Bouman was often encouraged by her father, a professor of electrical engineering, to explore scientific pursuits. One of her earliest memories of doing science was constructing and launching a tissue-paper hot-air balloon with him. Through middle and high school science projects analyzing fingerprint images and investigating whether people all perceive colors in the same way, Bouman developed an early interest in images and visual perception that would eventually lead her to study in the field of computational imaging. Bouman earned her bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the University of Michigan in 2011 and later completed her master's and doctoral studies in electrical engineering and computer science at MIT in 2017. Prior to Caltech, she was a postdoctoral fellow with the Event Horizon Telescope, which published the first picture of a black hole in 2019.
Starting at 6 p.m., members of Katie Bouman's lab will be present to answer questions about their research.
About the series
The Watson Lectures offer new opportunities each month to hear how Caltech researchers are tackling society's most pressing challenges and inventing the technologies of the future. Join a community of curiosity outside Beckman Auditorium to enjoy food, drinks, and music together before each lecture. Interactive displays related to the evening's topic will give audience members additional context and information. The festivities start at 6 p.m. Guests are also encouraged to stay for post-talk coffee and tea as well as the chance to chat with attendees and researchers.
Watson Lectures are free and open to the public.
Advance registration for Bouman's talk is full. Guests who have not registered are still welcome to attend the preshow, which does not require registration, beginning at 6 p.m., featuring food, music, and interactive displays.
After the preshow, non-ticketed guests interested in attending the talk may join our standby line by 6:50 p.m.
A recording will be made available on our YouTube channel.
Learn more about the topic at Katie Bouman's speaker page.

title: Brazil's presidential elections linked to decades of fluctuating environmental destruction – study
author: Fred Lewsey
summary: A University of Cambridge-led analysis of maps made from satellite imagery covering over three decades and seven presidents shows how the winner of Brazil’s national elections since 1990 directly affected the preservation of its globally vital ecosystems.
text:
A study tracking 35 years of vegetation data from the Amazon to the Cerrado over seven presidencies shows how Brazil’s top political leadership can dramatically slow down or speed up the loss of tropical forests and savannas.
          Brazil has shown the world that deforestation can be dramatically reduced when there is the political will to act. But that progress is fragile...
Vinicius Tonetti
A University of Cambridge-led analysis of maps made from satellite imagery covering over three decades and seven presidents shows how the winner of Brazil’s national elections since 1990 directly affected the preservation of its globally vital ecosystems.
The study reveals a rollercoaster of habitat loss rates across presidencies in the country's three largest biomes – the Amazon, Cerrado, and Atlantic Forest – from a peak of 3.62 million hectares of native vegetation vanishing annually under Itamar Franco in the nineties, to a low of just 1.21 million hectares a year under Temer a decade ago.
Researchers found that the Amazon lost an average of around 994,000 hectares annually during the first three years of Luiz Inácio ‘Lula’ da Silva's current presidency, compared with 1.4 million hectares a year under his predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro.
This represents a reduction of about 29% in the average annual area of Amazon lost under Lula’s return compared with Bolsonaro’s time in office, according to the study, published in Environmental Research Communications.
However, in the Cerrado, the vast tropical savannas of central Brazil, the trend moved in the opposite direction. Annual habitat losses averaged around 1.28 million hectares between 2023 and 2025, an increase of around 50% compared with 854,000 hectares per year under Bolsonaro, during whose presidency savanna loss accelerated.
The Cerrado, a vital source of water that feeds many of Brazil’s rivers, has seen major increases in commercial farming of crops such as soybean, as US-China trade tensions during Trump’s first term saw China pivot to Brazilian soybean.
Weaker legal protections, along with efforts to curb deforestation in the Amazon, may have pushed agricultural expansion into the Cerrado, say researchers. They warn that major soy traders’ withdrawal from a moratorium on growing soy on recently deforested land could have devastating consequences for Brazil’s natural habitats.
The study also reveals how the Atlantic Forest, which stretches along Brazil's eastern coastline but has been “highly fragmented” by centuries of farming and urbanisation, actually experienced periods of recovery rather than simply a slowdown in loss.
During Lula's first two terms, the Atlantic Forest gained an average of around 18,000 hectares of native vegetation a year. Under Rousseff, that figure rose to nearly 30,000 hectares annually. Since Rousseff left office, the Atlantic Forest has returned to net vegetation losses, although at a much smaller scale than in the Amazon or Cerrado.
It is the only one of Brazil's three major biomes to have experienced periods of net vegetation gain in the last thirty-five years.
“Brazilian presidents have dictated the fate of the country’s forests and savannas for over three decades,” said study lead author Dr Vinicius Tonetti, a Brazilian conservation biologist at the University of Cambridge’s Department of Zoology.
“We see that presidential terms characterised by strong environmental laws, satellite monitoring, and zero-deforestation agreements are clearly linked to major reductions in habitat loss,” Tonetti said. “Brazil's recent history shows just how much environmental policy matters and comes from the top.”
"Our findings also show that while deforestation in the Amazon has slowed under Lula, the loss of natural habitats across the Cerrado has remained high. Protecting one ecosystem while losing another is not a sustainable solution."
The study used land-cover maps from the MapBiomas project, derived from decades of satellite data, to track changes in the Amazon, Cerrado and Atlantic Forest between 1990 and 2025.
Across all three biomes combined, the largest average annual net loss of native vegetation occurred during the presidency of Itamar Franco, between 1993 and 1994, when approximately 3.62 million hectares disappeared each year.
Fernando Henrique Cardoso's (FHC) administration, from 1995 to 2002, recorded average annual losses of around 3.30 million hectares.
Lula's first two terms, between 2003 and 2010, marked a major turning point, with loss of natural habitat falling by some 35% to an annual average of around 2.44 million hectares. In the Amazon alone, habitat loss was around 20% lower under Lula than under FHC, with a significant slowdown in the rate of deforestation.
“During Lula's first two terms, agricultural production expanded while stronger monitoring and enforcement resulted in more habitat preservation,” said Tonetti. “Economic development and environmental protection do not have to come at the expense of each other."
Under Lula’s successor Dilma Rousseff, overall habitat loss almost halved again (a further 46% reduction) to about 1.31 million hectares a year, before reaching just 1.21 million hectares a year on average during Michel Temer's time in office.
Under Bolsonaro, however, major cuts to environment agencies, weakened enforcement, reduced environmental fines, and efforts to loosen environmental regulations coincided with a sharp loss of native vegetation across ecosystems, rising to 2.36 million hectares per year on average, almost doubling (95% increase) from the historic low of Temer’s premiership.
While Lula’s return saw deforestation in the Amazon fall significantly, the overall loss of native vegetation across Brazil’s three major biomes has declined by only around 2%, largely because of increasing vegetation loss in the Cerrado.
The collapse of the soy moratorium in the Amazon and new laws restricting Indigenous land claims are part of a worrying trend that may escalate under a new president, according to Tonetti. For example, Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged to overhaul the environmental licensing system if elected.
"Brazil has shown the world that deforestation can be dramatically reduced when there is the political will to act. But that progress is fragile. Recent changes to environmental legislation and the weakening of commitments to deforestation-free soy could undermine years of conservation gains,” said Tonetti.
“As the nation once again elects a president, the voters of Brazil need to understand just how much is at stake for some of the world’s most precious forests and ecosystems.”
The single largest gap in vegetation loss between presidents for any of the biomes was seen in the Amazon, which lost an average of 1.95 million hectares a year under Fernando Henrique Cardoso but just 614,158 hectares a year under Dilma Rousseff – an area of forest the size of Montenegro spared annually.

title: Good growth: Innovate Cambridge Summit 2026
author: Sarah Fell
summary: New analysis from Cambridge Innovation Capital (CIC), published ahead of the Summit, showed the average equity raised per deal across both life sciences and deep tech has increased five-fold in the last decade, with Cambridge-based early-stage companies having raised £9.1 billion in that period.
text:
More than 500 businesses, start-ups, innovators, academics, political and civic leaders attended the fifth Innovate Cambridge Summit. Speakers celebrated an extraordinary year for innovation in Cambridge, including the creation of three Cambridge-born unicorns, while emphasising the need for innovation-led growth to benefit everyone in the City and wider region.
New analysis from Cambridge Innovation Capital (CIC), published ahead of the Summit, showed the average equity raised per deal across both life sciences and deep tech has increased five-fold in the last decade, with Cambridge-based early-stage companies having raised £9.1 billion in that period.
Taking leadership in innovation
Professor Deborah Prentice, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Cambridge reflected on what makes Cambridge such a thriving innovation economy and the importance of taking a proactive and global leadership role in driving innovation that works for everyone: “There are three ways in which Cambridge takes leadership: through research excellence, by acting as one ecosystem and through our partnerships with other places and organisations.”
These themes were echoed by speakers throughout the day, including Mayor Paul Bristow, Peter Freeman (Chair of the Greater Cambridge Development Corporation) and Roland Sinker (Chair of the Inclusive Innovation and Growth Review, University of Cambridge) with a recurring focus on breakthrough research, ambitious partnerships and a shared sense of purpose across the ecosystem.
Strengthening the life sciences ecosystem
Following GSK’s recent announcement that it will be moving its R&D headquarters to Cambridge in 2029, Chief Scientific Officer, Tony Wood spoke about the increasing need for collaboration in the life sciences and that by moving to Cambridge GSK will be able to create more opportunities to achieve breakthroughs in drug discovery and patient care.
Global ambitions for quantum computing
John Aston, Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Research at the University of Cambridge led a discussion considering the UK’s global leadership role in spearheading the development and application of quantum computing. The University’s partnership with IonQ, which next year will bring the UK’s first commercial scale quantum computer to Cambridge, combined with the University’s research strengths in both quantum and its potential applications, underpinned by the ecosystem’s strength in supporting commercialisation, means that Cambridge is uniquely placed to play a national – and global - leadership role.
City partnerships: Manchester and Cambridge
Faye Holland (Director, Cambridge x Manchester Partnership) described the increasing success of the partnership between Cambridge and Manchester in combining the regions’ complementary strengths to increase the UK’s global competitiveness. The pioneering model for this cross-city approach is now being championed by government and adopted by other city partnerships across the UK.
Keeping jobs and know-how in the UK
How to create the right conditions for start-ups to grow, scale and stay in the UK was explored, and the creation of a new task force announced by Pascal Levensohn (Chair of Cambridge Innovation Hub Global Advisory Board) to take forward a new approach (outlined in a white paper published ahead of the Summit) to keeping a company’s footprint in the UK even if it is acquired internationally.
The Summit also heard from some of Cambridge’s most successful start-ups including Nyobolt and T-Therapeutics (both of which spun out of the University with support from Cambridge Enterprise) as well as Pragmatic Semiconductors, Cambridge Aerospace and CuspAI.
Widening opportunities
Ensuring that innovation-led growth benefits everyone who lives and works in Cambridge and the wider region was a central and recurring theme. Included, a new initiative to create more opportunities for young people in Greater Cambridge was announced at the Summit, with organisations present asked to contribute opportunities such as workplace visits, work experience and mentoring.
Accelerating the energy transition
In a parallel session, leaders from across the Cambridge cleantech ecosystem discussed accelerating the UK's clean energy transition. Hosted by DESNZ, Innovate Cambridge and Cambridge Zero, and chaired by Professor Emily Shuckburgh, Chief Scientific Adviser at DESNZ, the session brought together experts from industry, investment, academia and government. Discussions explored the opportunities and barriers to scaling cleantech innovation and commercialisation, alongside the role that innovation clusters such as Cambridge can play in addressing national clean energy challenges.
Kathryn Chapman, CEO of Innovate Cambridge, summed up the day: "Cambridge is ranked second in the world for innovation intensity, the globally leading research and talent at the University of Cambridge underpins this intensity. When academic institutions, business leaders and government come together with a single, compelling vision for innovation - we can turn the research into jobs, investment, innovation and better quality of life for communities in our region and the UK."

title: Tackling diabetes with an electronic implant: how a tiny catalyst lowers blood sugar
author: Peter Rüegg, Corporate Communications
summary: Researchers at ETH Zurich have developed an implantable system that clears excess glucose from the blood. The method has proved successful in the lab.
text:
Tackling diabetes with an electronic implant: how a tiny catalyst lowers blood sugar
In brief
- ETH researchers have developed a new implantable system to treat type 2 diabetes.
- The system uses a specially developed catalyst to convert glucose into gluconate in the body, removing some of the excess glucose from further metabolism.
- In a laboratory experiment using 5 litres of glucose solution – roughly the volume of blood in the human body – and in separate tests in mice, the researchers showed that the device converted glucose as intended.
Type 2 diabetes is becoming increasingly common worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, it is often linked to obesity, a sedentary lifestyle and excess energy intake over many years. Although insulin injections can bring blood sugar levels down, they do not address the body’s chronic energy surplus. Insulin merely helps muscle cells take up glucose from the bloodstream, but if the body does not use that energy, the excess is converted into fat. This helps explain why many patients continue to gain weight despite treatment.
Now, a team led by Martin Fussenegger has developed a potential new way to treat diabetes: an implantable system that uses an electrically powered catalyst to lower blood glucose. Fussenegger is a professor in ETH Zurich’s Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering in Basel. The team’s findings have been published in external page Science.
New approach uses electronics instead of biomolecules
For years, the Basel-based team of researchers has been exploring ways to tackle diabetes with systems that regulate blood sugar. Earlier approaches relied on specially developed genetic networks. However, these systems depend on biological components, which pose additional challenges in areas such as immune tolerance, stability, manufacturing and regulatory approval.
The new system gets around this problem with a catalyst made entirely from inorganic materials, which needs no cells, enzymes or other biological components. It consists of graphite felt studded with gold nanoclusters, which are themselves decorated with even smaller platinum particles. The materials showed excellent biocompatibility in the experimental study, says Fussenegger. The team developed the catalyst’s nanostructured surface themselves.
The implant also contains an electronic control unit housed in a 3D-printed casing. Power is supplied wirelessly at a frequency of 13.56 MHz, which is internationally designated for industrial, scientific and medical applications.
Converting glucose into gluconate
The catalyst converts excess glucose in the blood into gluconate. This means that some of the glucose is no longer metabolised and stored in tissue, which also helps limit the build-up of body fat. The gluconate is then excreted in the urine.
The catalyst is controlled wirelessly through a closed-loop system. A standard glucose sensor, like those commonly worn on the upper arm by people with diabetes, continuously monitors glucose levels in the tissue. If blood sugar rises too high after a meal, the sensor sends a signal via Bluetooth to a smartphone or smartwatch. The smart device then activates the catalyst, which uses electrical energy to convert the glucose. Once glucose levels have fallen to the desired level, the device switches itself off automatically, protecting patients from dangerously low blood sugar.
Successfully tested in mice
In a laboratory experiment, Fussenegger’s team tested the system in a reservoir holding five litres of a glucose-containing nutrient solution – roughly the volume of blood in the human body. This showed that the catalyst was capable of converting glucose in this volume of solution. The researchers also tested the system in diabetic mice and found that the animals’ blood sugar could be precisely regulated. The mice lost weight, the implant was well tolerated and it operated reliably during a six-week period. “The system operates at a very low voltage, and our experiments showed no evidence of tissue damage from either electrical or thermal effects,” says Fussenegger. The team has not yet tested the device on humans.
Paradigm shift: from conventional drugs to an electronic device
Fussenegger sees the approach as a paradigm shift away from conventional drugs and towards scalable, electronically controlled treatments that can be integrated into digital environments such as the Internet of Things. “
For decades, we have treated diabetes by telling the body how to manage glucose. We are now showing that we can take control of glucose directly, using electronics rather than drugs,” he says. “And the catalyst only activates when glucose levels are too high.”
The team now plans to develop the system into a medical device. Because the glucose-lowering mechanism itself works without cells or enzymes, technical development could be more straightforward.
Another advantage is that the components needed to build such a device, including external control and wireless power transmission devices, have already been developed and are commercially available.
Reference
Maity D, Guha Ray P, Buchmann P, Charpin-El-Hamri G, Fussenegger M: Wireless electrocatalytic closed-loop system for drug-free management of diabesity, Science, 22. Oktober 2026, DOI: external page 10.1126/science.ady8560

title: Parting words from a scholar who stepped up
author: Christina Pazzanese
summary: Tomiko Brown-Nagin reflects on her work as Radcliffe dean and as leader of high-stakes University initiatives.
text:
When she arrived on campus in 2012 as a legal scholar and historian, Tomiko Brown-Nagin never envisioned that she would one day lead the Harvard Radcliffe Institute.
Now, after eight years as Radcliffe’s dean, during which she also chaired two major University-wide efforts, Brown-Nagin is preparing to join Stanford University next month as the James Quillen Dean of its Graduate School of Education. She will also hold an appointment as professor of law at the Stanford School of Law.
In his Aug. 5 announcement to the Harvard community, President Alan Garber thanked Brown-Nagin for her “many lasting contributions” to Harvard, calling her an “outstanding dean” and “exemplary scholar.”
At Radcliffe, Brown-Nagin, RI ’17, spearheaded the development and implementation of a strategic plan that both affirmed the institute’s history as Radcliffe College and charted a bold path forward. She expanded Harvard’s faculty with key hires through jointly appointed Radcliffe Professorships, strengthened Radcliffe’s celebrated fellowship program, and launched a leadership program that partners local high school students with Harvard undergraduate mentors.
In 2019, President Lawrence S. Bacow asked Brown-Nagin to lead a comprehensive inquiry into the history and lasting impact of Harvard’s ties to slavery. The committee’s 2022 report identified “difficult truths” and offered recommendations for reparative steps the University should undertake. Garber called Brown-Nagin’s leadership of the effort “as humane as it was rigorous,” saying it “reflected the best of what it means to be a scholar in service to a community, an institution, and a nation.”
More recently, amid tensions related to political protest and civil discourse, Brown-Nagin co-chaired the University’s Open Inquiry and Constructive Dialogue Working Group, which Garber called a “tremendous contribution” to ensuring an improved campus climate. In its report, the group examined reluctance among many students, faculty, and staff to participate fully in the free exchange of ideas and viewpoints for fear of social, professional, or legal consequences and proposed concrete strategies and techniques to encourage respectful debate on campus.
In addition to her leadership of Radcliffe, Brown-Nagin is the Daniel P.S. Paul Professor of Constitutional Law at Harvard Law School and a professor of history in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences. In 2022, she authored a widely acclaimed book on Constance Baker Motley, the groundbreaking civil rights attorney, politician, and federal judge. In this edited conversation, she reflects on her time at Harvard and looks ahead to a new chapter at Stanford.
Gazette: Education — access to education as a means to opportunity — has been a central theme in your work as a historian, as a legal scholar, as dean, and in your family’s history. Did that guide your decision to join Stanford and lead its Graduate School of Education?
Tomiko Brown-Nagin: Absolutely it did. I would not depart Harvard but for an opportunity that I consider unique and entirely consistent with my longstanding commitment to education, access, and opportunity.
It is a throughline of my work — as a scholar and as a university administrator — that is also evident in my forthcoming book, which is a study of the nation’s fits and starts toward opportunity. The book is a sweeping survey of American history that also incorporates the history of the Deep South state where I was born and part of my family’s history, and my own experiences as a student who experienced the integration of public schools during the 1970s.
It’s a book about the transformational power of education and the power of individuals to find common ground across difference. That effort to seek commonality is a commitment that’s deeply important to me and something that I’ve been thinking a lot about over the past couple of years. It’s no secret that these have been — and continue to be — challenging times for educational systems, including colleges and universities, and for all of us who have invested our time in these institutions. We are being tested.
In your note to the Radcliffe community, you said in this new role, you “will be in a position to strengthen American education.” Where is American education today and what needs to be done?
Learning is declining, as evidenced by test scores since 2013. Researchers refer to the phenomenon as a “learning recession.”
In light of this trend, I’m eager to lead a faculty where a tremendous number and variety of researchers are pursuing projects that can illuminate why we are experiencing learning loss and can offer policy and legal recommendations. It fits my own interests so well. I’m looking forward to being a part of that — particularly now, when we are also experiencing disruption in education as a result of technological change, including AI. We really need to think deeply about what education is and what it is to become, and to speak in a way that can guide institutions that reflect the vast diversity of our education system. One of the first things that I will do at Stanford is lead a strategic planning process that I hope will help us speak to some of these issues.
You took on some of Harvard’s most complex challenges as chair of the Presidential Committee on Harvard and the Legacy of Slavery and as co-chair of the Working Group on Academic Freedom and Constructive Dialogue. Looking back, did those efforts accomplish what you had hoped?
President Bacow asked me to lead the first phase of the Harvard and Legacy of Slavery Initiative, which was focused on research. The charge that he put to me and the committee was to follow the evidence surrounding this very painful chapter in Harvard’s history and to make recommendations for how to move forward.
I’m very proud of the work that we were able to do. It was a monumental effort. It involved a lot of people: The committee included experts and faculty from every Harvard School. During the effort, I engaged the Harvard Corporation, vice presidents, the Harvard Board of Overseers, deans, faculty, students — virtually every stakeholder group that one can imagine — around that very difficult subject. It was not a foregone conclusion that we would be successful. The matter is fraught and frankly, not a lot of people other than a subset of scholars are interested in engaging with a subject that is so painful. Nevertheless, we were able to accomplish our scholarly mission.
As to the Open Inquiry work, I was asked by President Garber and Provost [John F.] Manning to take on that role with my colleague Eric Beerbohm, and I do think that our report successfully articulated aspirations for what our learning community should look like. We suggested tools and techniques for moving the University toward a better learning climate, things like the Chatham House Rule and new skills-building efforts across the Schools to teach students as well as educators how to engage with controversial issues in a constructive manner. I’m very pleased that Harvard approached that issue in the way that it did.
Radcliffe introduced the Emerging Leaders Program for high school students to work with College students to develop and hone their leadership skills. Why was that so important to initiate?
Universities like Harvard directly serve a very small and exclusive group of students. And yet it seems to me that while a relatively few students will have the benefits of an elite research education, institutions like Radcliffe can and should serve local communities and introduce a broader cross section of students to the life of the mind, to deep research, to interacting with serious scholars and students. And that’s what I have tried to do during my time at Radcliffe.
The Emerging Leaders Program is a leadership program, but it’s also a research program. One thing that makes it distinctive is that the undergraduates and the high schoolers learn about leadership using the collections of the Schlesinger Library — we introduce these students to archival research. It’s such an important learning tool, and it’s a creative way that our staff members and our students engage these high school students in thinking about how they can contribute productively to whatever social reform issues they find compelling. We also teach them about women leaders, which is important to me and important to us as an institution at Radcliffe.
As you prepare to leave Cambridge, what do you think you’ll miss most?
I will miss Harvard deeply. And I am filled with gratitude for the opportunities that I’ve had to help strengthen this great university. I’m so grateful to Larry Bacow, Drew Faust, and Alan Garber for the opportunities they gave me at Radcliffe. I’m a scholar first, and it never occurred to me that my scholarly path would lead me to this administrative role.
I’m also grateful for the opportunity to have served with a wonderful group of deans during very challenging circumstances. And although I am going on to a different institution, I would like to think that through the relationships that I’ve built over 14 years, and the work that I’ve done, I will remain connected to Harvard. Wherever I am in the world, I will always be a champion of Harvard and of Radcliffe.

title: Time to leave?
author: Samantha Laine Perfas
summary: ‘Case for Quitting’ author Lindsay Crouse on why you’re wrong when you answer ‘persevere’
text:
You’ve probably heard some version of the message: “Don’t be a quitter.” But in journalist Lindsay Crouse’s new book, “The Case for Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Out,” she argues that giving up sometimes is the best decision. In an interview with the Gazette, which has been edited for clarity and length, Crouse ’06 discussed the benefits of learning when to say “enough is enough.”
Gazette: What made you question your own relationship with quitting?
Lindsay Crouse: A lot of us grow up embracing but never questioning the language of ambition: to go harder, keep going, do more, never give up. That was always my recipe for how to achieve my dreams. And it worked, to a certain degree. I grew up in a small town, went to Harvard, ran marathons. I moved to New York and eventually landed a job at The New York Times, where I reported on how perseverance helps us achieve our goals. I viewed quitting as the opposite of perseverance, almost like a flaw of weaker people compared to the superpower of perseverance for the successful.
But perseverance and quitting are not opposites; in fact, quitting is a tool of perseverance. I wanted to explore the value of learning to stop and how it can help you create not just a happy and balanced life but also help you succeed in ways that are more fulfilling.
In your book you mention the Finnish concept of sisu, the grim determination to push through adversity. How can sisu be a double-edged sword?
Sisu can be a superpower, but it can become a weakness when it’s misapplied to problems that should be questioned or challenged. That’s when sisu can become harmful. Researchers in Finland like Amelia Latu have done a lot of research on how sisu is beneficial for us. It helps us thrive. It builds our resilience. But harmful sisu can hold us back. It can isolate us or cause us to overlook our problems. It can also make us blame other people for having problems. Sisu is great when we need help overcoming problems, but it can also cause us to ignore situations in which we’d be better off quitting.
Why does wanting to quit sometimes feel like a character flaw?
We think of quitting as a passive action or thing that happens to us. Our culture doesn’t always make room for the idea of quitting as an active choice, of taking control of a situation where we might not have control. I would argue that quitting (in many cases) is one of the boldest agentic decisions you can make.
One example: Let’s say you’re middle-aged. You’re well established, but you look at the trajectory of where you’ll be in five or 10 years. Do you like what you see? If not, how is it going to change? It often requires quitting something that you’re doing. But again, our culture rewards continuing. It rewards completion, and quitting is the opposite of that. It’s countercultural to make the decision to not continue your current path.
“Our culture doesn’t always make room for the idea of quitting as an active choice, of taking control of a situation where we might not have control.”
Lindsay Crouse
What is the harm in not quitting when you should?
In the long run, if we want to do our best, we need to learn to quit. When we fail to quit, we waste precious resources — like our time, our energy, our money — on quests that will make us increasingly miserable while often falling short of what we want. We invest those resources in paths that don’t succeed. In my own life, I’ve been tormented by the tension between productive hard work and working pointlessly hard. They can feel the same, but they get very different outcomes. Focusing on work alone keeps us from registering the mounting costs of that work, especially when it’s achieving nothing.
In the book you ask if women should quit like men. Should they?
I wrote an article in 2018 for The New York Times detailing women’s abilities to persevere in brutal circumstances, in this case the Boston Marathon. Women have physical, mental, and social qualities that help us to endure more and quit less than men; that’s especially true when conditions are harsh and the stakes are high. But the question is, does this help women? Who benefits from women’s ability to endure?
It’s often not women, it’s everybody else.
Women live longer than men, but we don’t necessarily live better. We’re more likely to battle chronic pain, to experience insomnia, to suffer migraines, to take meds for anxiety and depression. Women graduate from school at higher rates than men, but our incomes haven’t gone up. We seldom occupy the C-suite. Motherhood is another arena where we keep showing up, keep going harder, and keep doing more. I think it’s fair to say that women sometimes look at life like a war of attrition, where suffering is success. But that’s not true. Suffering is not success, and we wind up with more suffering and less reward.
Let’s say I’m tempted to quit something, be it a relationship, a job, a goal. How can I tell if it’s the kind of impulse I should listen to or if it’s a situation where it might benefit me to keep going?
When we want to quit something, it’s common to have an impulsive response: I can’t. Why not? Is it because you want to avoid the pain of disruption or is it actually true? Maybe you’re not in a position to quit right now. But can you take active steps toward building yourself an off-ramp? Maybe it’s financial, a lifestyle adjustment, a gap in your skill set. Take steps to build that cushion for a softer landing in your quest for something else. It’s also important to think about what it is you’re trying to leave or quit. Is it the environment? Your team? The job itself? Your role or workload? It’s a process of figuring out what you want to leave, figuring out if you can change it, and finally figuring out where you’ll go next.
How can we change our relationship with quitting so that we view it as a potential form of liberation rather than failure?
Just as quitting is a choice, so is continuing. These are equal decisions. And it’s important to acknowledge that while quitting does give you that liberation, it doesn’t necessarily tell you what to do next. You need to either be at peace with that or take steps to mitigate the risks involved.
I think oftentimes when we look at quitting, we say, “I don’t know how bad it will be, when I don’t know what’s coming next.” I think we forget that we also don’t know how good it could be. Look at quitting with the same optimism that we might apply to continuing. I think these are all ways to give the act of quitting equal weight in our lives. We can think about what it can bring us, as opposed to simply what we’re going to lose.

title: New UK trial aims to find answers more quickly for Alzheimer's disease
author: Eliza  Kania, Samantha Rey
summary: Multi-site trial will test several drugs simultaneously and drop those not showing clear benefit.
text:
Health
Multi-site trial will test several drugs simultaneously and drop those not showing clear benefit.
An innovative national trial has been launched that could cut years from the search for treatments that work for people with Alzheimer’s disease, the most common type of dementia. Minister of State for Health and Social Care Alison McGovern MP marked the launch with a visit to the trial site at Charing Cross Hospital in London.
The AD-SMART trial is led by the UK Dementia Research Institute (UK DRI) at Imperial College London and by Alzheimer’s Research UK, in partnership with the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), the Medical Research Council (MRC) and Health Data Research UK (HDR UK). Ongoing funding has been committed by the UK government.
Alzheimer’s affects around 600,000 people in the UK and there are currently no NHS treatments that can slow or stop the underlying disease.
Applying lessons from cancer to dementia
AD-SMART (Alzheimer's disease Systematic Multi-arm Adaptive Randomised Trial) will test multiple drugs simultaneously, with separate groups of participants each beginning treatment with a different drug. Unusually, all groups will be compared with one single group of participants taking a placebo.
Researchers will examine whether the medicines can lessen symptoms such as memory and thinking problems and help people maintain their quality of life as the disease progresses. As the trial continues, regular checking of results will allow any drug that doesn't show clear benefit to be dropped quickly and replaced with another candidate.
For too long, Alzheimer’s research has moved at the pace of one drug, one trial, one answer, sometimes taking a decade or more before we know if we’ve found something that works. We are applying advances from cancer and other conditions to accelerate testing of treatments for people with Alzheimer’s disease.  Professor Paresh Malhotra Study lead, Group Leader at the UK DRI Centre for Care Research & Technology at Imperial College London
The trial will start with two repurposed medicines already approved for use to treat type 2 diabetes and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), Because the drugs are already approved for other conditions and have a well-established safety profile, if they prove successful, they could reach people living with Alzheimer’s much faster than a medicine developed from scratch.
As well as repurposed drugs, the trial is also designed to test new potential treatments coming through the research pipeline.
Study lead Professor Paresh Malhotra, Group Leader at the UK DRI Centre for Care Research & Technology at Imperial College London, said: “For too long, Alzheimer’s research has moved at the pace of one drug, one trial, one answer, sometimes taking a decade or more before we know if we’ve found something that works. We are applying advances from cancer and other conditions to accelerate testing of treatments for people with Alzheimer’s disease."
Professor Siddharthan Chandran, Director of the UK Dementia Research Institute, said: “We already know this model works. The SMART approach, used by us in Motor Neurone Disease in MND-SMART, has shown that testing multiple drugs at once, in one smart trial design, can speed up the testing of new treatments for neurodegenerative conditions. Now, we’re doing the same for Alzheimer’s."
“And because of the way SMART trials are designed, biotech and pharmaceutical companies can also bring their drugs straight into the trial. That means more treatments tested more quickly, and for people living with Alzheimer’s, that could make all the difference.”
Breakthroughs that change people’s lives
Dementia is one of the most pressing medical and societal challenges, affecting almost one million people in the UK. According to Alzheimer’s Society, this number is projected to rise to 1.4 million by 2040.
The UK Prime Minister, Andy Burnham MP, has spoken publicly of his own father's battle with Alzheimer's disease. He said of the trial: “I know how it feels to lose a loved one to dementia and have seen first-hand the devastating impact this illness has on families. That’s why I’m proud to see this trial being launched in the UK, so that cutting-edge treatments can reach patients here as soon as possible."
He added: “I have made dementia research a national priority. I want Britain to be the leading nation, making the breakthroughs that change people’s lives.”
UK Science Minister Chris McDonald MP said: “AD-SMART will help to uncover new treatments faster by exploring how existing drugs might be used to treat dementia, giving hope that we might be able to find ways to improve patients’ quality of life in the future.”
Dr Sheona Scales, Director of Research at Alzheimer’s Research UK, said: “For people living with Alzheimer’s disease, time is precious. We urgently need more treatment options that can help people live better for longer and stay connected to the people they love."
I have made dementia research a national priority. I want Britain to be the leading nation, making the breakthroughs that change people’s lives. Andy Burnham MP The UK Prime Minister
AD-SMART is designed to find effective treatments sooner. As a multi-arm, multi-stage platform trial, by testing several drugs at once against a single shared placebo group, more participants receive an active treatment than would do in a traditional trial.
Results are reviewed at regular stages, and drugs showing no benefit are dropped and replaced with new ones, meaning that fewer people receive ineffective treatments. Sharing one placebo group can also more than halve the time needed to evaluate treatments, which reduces costs.
Minister’s visit
On Wednesday 21 October, Alison McGovern MP, Minister of State at the Department of Health and Social Care, visited the AD-SMART trial site at the Imperial Memory Unit, Charing Cross Hospital, part of Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust. During the visit, the Minister met Professor Paresh Malhotra, a trial participant and members of the AD-SMART trial team.
The trial is being delivered by a team at Imperial College London, the UCL Innovative Clinical Trials Unit and the MRC Centre of Research Excellence in Clinical Trial Innovation (UCL), the University of Oxford and Dementias Platform UK (DPUK), with support from leading Alzheimer’s experts across the UK.

title: AI minister announces measures to protect against AI risks in speech at Imperial
author: Joanna Wilson
summary: The Rt Hon Kanishka Narayan MP, Minister for Artificial Intelligence, announced a suite of measures to better protect Britain from the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI during an event at Imperial.
text:
Health
The Rt Hon Kanishka Narayan MP, Minister for Artificial Intelligence, announced a suite of measures to better protect Britain from the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI during an event at Imperial.
The speech was given at Base One, an innovation space by Imperial which is supporting deep tech companies to scale and grow. Base One is part of Imperial’s Old Oak Innovation Cluster and sits at the heart of WestTech London, the innovation ecosystem established and anchored by Imperial which brings together world-class research, global talent, industry and infrastructure to create jobs, attract investment, drive growth and cement the UK’s position as a leader in science and technology.
The Rt Hon Kanishka Narayan MP, Minister for Artificial Intelligence, announced a suite of measures to better protect Britain from the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI, with the government urgently putting frontier AI to work strengthening cyber defences, examining stronger legal protections and preparing for serious incidents involving autonomous AI systems.
Imperial is focused on ensuring that frontier AI is developed and deployed safely and responsibly, with governance, safeguards, and real-world impact embedded from the outset.  Professor Peter Haynes Provost and Deputy President, Imperial College London
The move builds on two pilots that have already helped identify and fix over a thousand potential cyber vulnerabilities across government systems, and detect potential cyber threats. Extending the programme will help protect public services that people rely on every day and will support longer-term adoption across the public sector.
The Minister argued for a whole-society approach to resilience in the face of emerging AI risks, so that this technology continues to serve British people’s interests and boost our prosperity, as well as our security.
AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said: “I want Britain to become one of the hardest countries in the world to attack using artificial intelligence. We will use every power at our disposal. We will legislate wherever necessary. And we won’t look to law alone. We will look to British ingenuity: our scientific expertise, technological capabilities and institutions to understand these increasingly powerful systems, defend against emerging threats and respond when things go wrong.
“And to the companies developing the world’s most powerful AI systems, my message is: Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system.”
Professor Peter Haynes, Provost of Imperial College London, said: “Here at Imperial, we have AI experts in computer science, engineering, the natural sciences, medicine, and business developing cutting-edge research and innovation.
“Their work frequently leads to impactful applications, from accelerating drug discovery and improving healthcare to advancing climate modelling, designing advanced materials, securing infrastructure and creating trustworthy human-centred AI systems.”
He added: “Imperial is focused on ensuring that frontier AI is developed and deployed safely and responsibly, with governance, safeguards, and real-world impact embedded from the outset.
“And finally, with an eye firmly on the future, we’re investing in a new facility at our White City Deep Tech Campus that will bring together researchers from multiple disciplines to create a powerful engine for data science, AI and machine learning.”
Imperial’s work in AI includes:
- The university’s new Academic Building, to be built at our White City Deep Tech Campus, which will bring together academic researchers from across disciplines at an unprecedented scale to create a powerful engine for data science, AI and machine learning.
- A new Centre for AI-Driven Innovation, established jointly with the World Economic Forum and supported by the UK Government, which is dedicated to developing and scaling novel AI applications across key growth sectors of the UK’s industrial strategy. It is the first WEF Global Centre to be based in the UK.
- The School of Convergence Science has a major focus on Human and Artificial Intelligence, and will help to shape a responsible, collaborative AI landscape that amplifies human creativity, intelligence and societal impact while ensuring human empowerment. It will augment the intelligence of humans and machines to help humanity thrive.
- The Frontier AI Lab, recently established with Thomson-Reuters, is a landmark strategic partnership between industry and our School of Convergence Science that is focused on addressing the safety, reliability, and societal and economic impacts of AI.

title: At MIT, Martha Minow speaks on sustaining democracy, both by using and overcoming AI
author: Peter Dizikes | MIT News
summary: Harvard Law School Professor Martha Minow delivered MIT’s Compton Lecture, examining the current threats to democracy, the challenges to it present by AI, and possible ways that AI could better inform people and have civic value.
text:
Legal scholar Martha Minow delivered this fall’s Compton Lecture at MIT on Thursday, examining the civic foundations of democracy — and describing how artificial intelligence is undermining it, but could be used to help reinforce traditional U.S. governance.
“It’s not a good time for democracy or constitutionalism,” said Minow, who is the 300th Anniversary University Professor at Harvard University, and a prominent expert in constitutional law and human rights. She noted a litany of challenges to democracy in recent years, including violations of laws and norms, the stifling of free speech, a diminution of congressional authority, disregard of legal rulings, the common vilification of others in society, and more.
Recent Gallup polling, Minow observed, shows 77 percent of people saying that the founders of the U.S. would be disappointed in the contemporary condition of the country.
“Many people genuinely wonder whether this nation’s system of government and rule of law, ignited 250 years ago, will survive,” Minow said.
Her remarks assessed the state of the U.S. in terms of what she called four key “ingredients” of democracy: education, reliable and accessible information, security from violence, and fairness. Minow evaluated how AI has, among other things, influenced these areas of life — but also suggested ways people could use contemporary technology to help.
“It’s very familiar to hear blame attributed to digital technologies and experts of all stripes, but a turnaround, I believe, is genuinely possible if people at MIT and elsewhere pour time and talent towards real and much-needed solutions,” Minow said.
A substantial portion of her remarks focused on the pitfalls of AI in education. That issue compounds some other troubling trends: The U.S. already has large local and regional disparities in educational funding, Minow noted, while schools have actually become significantly more segregated in economic and ethnic terms over the last three decades.
In this context, AI threatens to further weaken independent-thinking skills, Minow suggested, just when greater understanding of civic issues is absolutely vital.
“As AI surges, I think we have to learn to be smarter about how to use it, how to regulate it, and how to actually educate people about the costs of mindless using,” Minow said. She added: “Dominant AI platforms supercharge the strategies that are deployed by social media companies, inducing passivity in people … Leading AI models and interfaces and sycophantic elements endanger the development particularly of young people’s capabilities to think, to remember, and to engage in critical thinking.”
That trend away from cognitive effort, she suggested, can be changed — perhaps through AI tools that act more like tutors and are designed to enhance people’s deep thinking.
“Existing LLMs, model training, and interface design can offer nudges and questions and hints rather than replacing student work, but there’s so much more that could be developed, and more effectively, to be trustworthy, and to deepen human activities and curiosity, rather than replacing people,” Minow said.
To the audience, she added, “AI tools could do much more of that … And I believe that you, the people here, could develop better tools than the ones that are out there. And make better assessments, more meaningful and cheating-resistant.”
Minow’s talk, “Constituting Democracy in the Era of AI,” was delivered to a large audience in MIT’s Huntington Hall, Room 10-250 on campus.
MIT President Sally A. Kornbluth delivered introductory remarks to the audience. The Karl Taylor Compton Lecture Series, introduced in 1957, is the highest-profile event of its kind at MIT. Karl Taylor Compton was MIT’s ninth president, serving from 1930 to 1948, and then becoming chair of the MIT Corporation from 1948 to 1954.
“He guided MIT through the Great Depression and World War II,” Kornbluth said, “transforming the Institute from an outstanding school for training job-ready engineers to a great global research university.”
She added: “He was also a deeply committed patriot who helped harness the intellectual power of America’s research universities to serve the nation during World War II.”
Kornbluth called Minow “a legal scholar of extraordinary intellectual scope,” and a “dedicated educator whose work has shaped how we think about the law and our own humanity, as individuals and as a society.”
Minow has been a faculty member at Harvard Law School since 1981, and served as dean of the school from 2009 through 2017. Minow earned her BA in history from the University of Michigan, an MA in education from Harvard, and a JD from Yale University.
Minow’s books include “Making All the Difference” (1990), “Partners Not Rivals” (2002), and “When Should Law Forgive?” (2020).
In her talk, Minow also discussed the civic effects of misinformation, threats of violence, and multiple dimension of societal fairness. Modern media technology has led to a 75 percent reduction in journalists in recent decades, Minow observed, with an attendant rise in corruption in places without local media. Civic-minded technologists, she proposed, should work towards establishing a widely-used “information commons,” or many forms of them, to help people access more reliable information.
Meanwhile, when it comes to basic security in society, Minow warned, “We’re on the brink right now. I know a lot of judges, and every one of them has a credible threat of violence against them. In America. This is not acceptable.”
For all the challenges to democracy and traditional civic norms, however, Minow sounded positive notes throughout her remarks, pointing out that there are many opportunities to create new forms of reliable information, education, and community relations.
“We have to actually invent the world that we want to live in,” she offered.
Minow’s remarks were followed by a Q&A session in which Kornbluth read aloud questions submitted by the audience — and asked her to characterize her concerns about present trends.
“I worry about the loss of the Enlightenment,” Minow said. “I worry about the loss of the belief that reason, and testing hypotheses, and rejecting myths in the face of evidence, and the toleration and rights and expansion of participation that came along with the Enlightenment, that’s what concerns me the most. That’s why the disinformation issue for me is so important, that’s why the loss of critical thinking in schools is so important.”
She added: “I’ve spent much of my own career thinking about mass violence. What happens when people don’t understand each other, and are afraid. And it’s terrible, and we don’t want to be there. And I do view the Enlightenment as a time when people learned that actually having mass wars is a bad thing, and coming up with toleration is a good thing, and testing our ideas in light of evidence other people can share can produce a better life for everybody. I worry we’re abandoning that right now.”

title: Reinforcing the value of human understanding at MIT
author: Benjamin Daniel | School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences
summary: During the MIT School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Science's 75th Anniversary Symposium, scholars, students, and performers from across SHASS gathered to celebrate its legacy and contributions.
text:
At the MIT School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS) 75th Anniversary Symposium, speakers celebrated the school’s value and contributions, while exploring how artificial intelligence is transforming many aspects of teaching, research, and society.
The symposium was held Sept. 24-25 in the Linde Music Building’s Thomas Tull Concert Hall. Scholars, students, staff, and alumni from across SHASS and MIT gathered for the event, which kicked off with welcoming remarks from MIT leadership.
“How should we think about MIT’s School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences? With enthusiastic appreciation and gratitude,” said President Sally Kornbluth.
The school’s origins date back to the Lewis Committee Report, commissioned by MIT and published in 1949, which called for stronger integration between scientific and technical topics and humanistic scholarship and teaching.
Kornbluth noted that, much like when the school was founded just after World War II, the world faces uncertainty as it grapples with the broad implications of artificial intelligence.
“AI has suddenly arrived with enormous consequences for both research and education,” she said. “As we face the challenges of our own time, and our own society, it’s clear that MIT has never needed your particular insight and guidance more than we do now.”
In opening remarks, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan described the importance of a human-centered approach to technology, one that considers both its efficacy and its impacts. He lauded many of the new research projects happening through the MIT Human Insight Collaborative, a strategic initiative launched in 2024.
“Today — a time of rapid, AI-driven change — the arts, humanities, and social sciences are as important as ever,” he said. “To be able to contribute effectively to solving the world’s great challenges, it is not enough to gain technical mastery.”
Chancellor Melissa Nobles recalled how, during her tenure as SHASS dean from 2015 to 2021, reading the positive feedback from students in their SHASS course assessments reinforced the value of the school’s teaching.
“MIT students have a range of interests that draw them to our classes that may be invisible to their STEM professors, but that we very well know our students have,” said Nobles, who is also a professor of political science.
Agustín Rayo, the Kenan Sahin Dean of SHASS and professor of philosophy, noted that, while research in the school plays a key role in addressing global issues such as climate change and AI, the value of the work in SHASS should not be measured by practical application alone.
“Education should also help us ask what is worth doing, what do we owe one another, and what makes a life worth living,” Rayo said. “Some research matters because it helps us understand the histories, cultures, and social structures that have made us who we are. Some things matter because they enrich human life.”
Scholarship from across SHASS and beyond
Over the symposium’s two days, research presentations, panel discussions, and performances offered attendees opportunities to engage with the role of SHASS in exploring today’s biggest societal questions.
“We gather not so much to look back over the past 75 years, but to showcase where we are now, and share what we urgently aim to tackle together in the years ahead,” said David Kaiser, Germeshausen Professor of the History of Science and professor of physics at MIT, who also served as chair of the symposium planning committee.
The first day included a session on teaching and learning innovations. Faculty presented on the success of educational programs housed within SHASS, including the MIT Indigenous Languages Initiative Master's Program, the Master in Data, Economics, and Design of Policy (DEDP), and MISTI, the hub for global experiences for MIT students.
Stephanie Seed, associate professor of literature, spoke about why she and others are working to reintegrate classic books into their teaching.
“MIT, of course, is an institution unusually oriented towards the future,” she said. “Our students are trained to imagine and create worlds that don’t yet exist. And it’s precisely this future orientation that makes reading the past especially important here.”
Eric Klopfer, professor of Comparative Media Studies/Writing and co-author of MIT’s recent report on AI and instruction, said this is a moment when instructors must reassess how courses are taught.
“I don’t know exactly what that looks like, but I do think it means something that’s more than modifying our curriculum. I think it really means rethinking what the educational experience is,” he said.
During a session on computing and society, panelists described different views and research into technology and how it affects humans.
“We project aspects of ourselves onto computational systems,” said MIT Professor D. Fox Harrell during his talk about seeing “selfness” in machines.
“What makes an AI system is not just the code, not just the programming or the algorithm, it’s the fact that we narrate it as being intentional,” he said.
Program in Science, Technology, and Society Professor Sherry Turkle offered a skeptical view of human-technology interaction, particularly with AI chatbots, which she describes as “intimate machines.”
“If social media came for our attention, I argue that chatbots are coming for our capacity for attachment, which is deeper and much more troubling,” said Turkle.
Professor David Autor, head of the Department of Economics, said it’s an exciting time to be working at MIT, where scholars are collaborating to explore AI’s impact on society.
“I don’t think there’s a close analogy to a moment when everyone felt the world change so quickly,” he said. “The stakes feel incredibly high.”
Celebrating the arts and engaging with the future
The first day concluded with a rousing Music and Theater Arts performance showcase, which began with an excerpt from Stan Lai’s “A Dream Like A Dream,” a play directed and performed by students and instructors in class 21T.100 (Theater Arts Production).
“Variations on the Theme of SHASS 75,” a piece choreographed by Dan Safer, senior lecturer and director of dance programs, combined movement, lighting, and music in a celebration of both the human body and the school’s milestone anniversary.
Student and faculty musicians from a variety of styles and disciplines shared the stage, including Rambax MIT, MIT Concert Choir, and the MIT All-Star Jazz Combo. The showcase included stirring renditions of “Madrigal,” composed by Vice Provost for the Arts Keeril Makan, and “Prayer for Peace.”
On the second day of the symposium, several alumni presented on their current work and the impact of their SHASS experiences.
Jessica Coon PhD ’10, now a professor of linguistics at McGill University, spoke about the leading role MIT Linguistics plays in preserving endangered languages, and how her studies at MIT prepared her to carry on that work.
“SHASS gives us the tools not just to conduct research, but to communicate the impacts of this research across a variety of different audiences and in different ways,” she said.
Ankita Reddy ’19 double-majored in anthropology and biology and is now an MD/PhD student at the University of Pennsylvania. She highlighted her most impactful SHASS courses, including 21A.308 (Global Mental Health).
“This was the first time I was forced to consider how good health care looks different based on social systems and cultural practices,” she said. “SHASS made me more comfortable with, and more curious about, complexity.”
During the symposium’s final session, panelists engaged in a conversation about AI, art, and the implications for creatives in an era where their art can be co-opted and copied.
“There’s so much praise for new and upgraded technologies,” remarked associate professor of literature Sandy Alexandre. “The question I consistently have is: What does it mean to be an upgraded human being? How are we innovating as technology is innovating?”
Philosopher Justin Khoo said AI’s role in art could be considered a “giant paint brush you don’t have much control over,” adding he could see the creation of new sub-genres of art that are human-only, AI-infused, and purely AI, for example.
Khoo closed by saying he encourages students to “think broadly, and really take seriously the humanistic education here at MIT.”
“A broad understanding of a set of concepts which are widely applicable, not just narrowly applicable, I think that’s what we need more than ever now,” he said.
As the symposium came to a close, attendee Kent Sahin praised the event.
“I’ve attended every session, and this is a fantastic program and a great celebration of the 75th anniversary,” he said. “Clearly, whether it’s AI impact, the impact of climate change, or the impact of political and social change, SHASS is in the right place at the right time.”

title: YST Cube opens at NUS, broadening horizons in music education
author: National University of Singapore
summary: NUS unveils the YST Cube, a flexible arts space that supports music education, performance and collaboration.
text:
YST Cube debuts new possibilities for music education and performance at NUS
Reimagining YST's former Orchestra Hall, the new flexible arts space gives students more room to learn, create and present their work.
For years, the Orchestra Hall at NUS' Yong Siew Toh Conservatory of Music (YST) served primarily as a venue for rehearsals and masterclasses. Now, the familiar space has been given a new lease of life.
Officially opened on 22 October 2026, the YST Cube is a 254sqm flexible arts space where students and faculty can explore different ways of creating, performing and experiencing music — part of YST's broader efforts to keep up with changing approaches to music education and artistic practice.
“The YST Cube will create new and exciting possibilities for students and faculty to experiment and push the boundaries of artistic practice,” said NUS President Professor Tan Eng Chye at the launch of the Cube during the opening ceremony of Performers(’) Present, YST's triennial international artistic research symposium.
“It will also be a convening space for visiting artists, educators and researchers from around the world to converge, create and showcase.”
Akin to black box performance spaces, the Cube can be reconfigured for different performance formats, including arrangements where audiences surround performers. Its integrated lighting, projection and acoustic systems also support multimedia performances and other artistic activities.
More room to create
For third-year Composition student Joel Tan, the Cube offers possibilities for exploring different ways of presenting music.
“Having the Cube would mean that the school has the capabilities to host much more ambitious projects and performances,” he said.
He is particularly interested in its lighting and projection capabilities, having had limited opportunities to explore these elements previously at YST.
Joel's interest in how audiences experience music is also reflected in a piece he is developing, which explores the individual components of sound, and how different parts of sound can come together as a whole. Using three speakers placed in separate rooms connected by a hallway, the piece allows listeners to experience the different sounds individually and how they merge, depending on how they move through the space.
For fourth-year student Chan Chen, who is pursuing Music, Collaboration and Production with a Second Major in Audio Arts & Sciences, the Cube has the potential to bridge the gap between developing artistic ideas and bringing them to life, while allowing him to further hone his technical skills.
Having previously experimented with audio-reactive visuals and soundscape installations in his first two years at YST, he is now developing an immersive multimedia concert experience that integrates live chamber music with real-time audio-reactive visuals for his final-year project.
Finding a suitable venue with the necessary technical infrastructure has been a challenge, particularly when multiple projectors are involved.
“The new YST Cube potentially addresses many of these challenges through its integrated projection capabilities and flexible performance configurations. It presents an exciting opportunity to explore ideas that might otherwise be difficult to realise within a traditional concert setting,” he shared.
Amplifying the arts
The Cube's opening coincided with the Performers(’) Present symposium, taking place from 22 to 25 October 2026. The symposium will occupy the main venue and its adjoining pre-function area, which can also function independently as a smaller event space.
Beyond music education, the Cube will broaden the range of artistic experiences available to students across different disciplines, in line with the university’s Arts for All framework.
It will also welcome arts organisations and external hirers for performances, rehearsals, creative residencies and collaborative projects, fostering artistic exchange and partnerships between YST and the local arts sector.
“The arts is a deeply fascinating and enriching discipline, and we want every student, whatever their discipline may be, to discover and learn about the arts,” said Prof Tan.
“They stretch our imagination, give us new lenses to see the world and deepen our understanding of the human experience.”

title: YST Cube opens at NUS
author: National University of Singapore
summary: NUS unveils the YST Cube, a flexible arts space repurposed from its former Orchestra Hall to support evolving approaches to music education and performance.
text:
YST Cube opens at NUS as a new space for evolving approaches to music education and performance
The space will offer students a future-ready environment for learning, artistic creation and collaboration, while supporting NUS’s wider commitment to the arts.
The Yong Siew Toh Conservatory of Music (YST) at the National University of Singapore (NUS) unveiled the YST Cube today, transforming its former Orchestra Hall into a flexible, reconfigurable arts space for music education, artistic creation, and performance. 
As approaches to artistic creation, learning and performance continue to evolve, students are exploring broader possibilities in how music can be created and presented, while taking greater ownership of their work. The transformation forms part of YST’s broader academic and artistic development, including reimagining how its physical spaces can support these changing approaches. By building on an existing space while expanding what it can enable, the Cube provides YST with greater capacity to respond to developments in music education over time. 
The Cube was officially opened by NUS President Professor Tan Eng Chye at the Opening Ceremony of Performers(’) Present, YST’s triennial international artistic research symposium, on 22 October 2026. 
“The YST Cube will create new and exciting possibilities for students and faculty to experiment and push the boundaries of artistic practice,” said Professor Tan. 
“It will also be a convening space for visiting artists, educators and researchers from around the world to converge, create and showcase.” 
The opening of the Cube strengthens YST’s role in the arts at NUS, advancing the University’s Arts for All (AFA) framework by broadening the range of artistic experiences that can take place on campus. While primarily serving NUS’s Music students, the new venue will also welcome the wider NUS community through public performances, presentations and other activities, creating further opportunities to engage with the arts at NUS. 
A flexible space for 21st century music education 
The Cube reimagines the Conservatory’s former Orchestra Hall – previously used primarily for orchestra rehearsals and masterclasses – as a purpose-built, flexible space for music education and performance. The transformation comes 20 years after the Conservatory building first opened. 
The Cube’s 254 sqm adaptable configuration, akin to black box performance spaces, allows it to be tailored to different uses, accommodating a range of performance formats, audience layouts and production requirements. For example, the Cube can shift between conventional performance formats and 360-degree arena-style setups where audiences surround the performers, or for multimedia work incorporating projection and lighting. 
Not only can it support conventional teaching, rehearsals and recitals, the new space can also accommodate workshops, presentations, multimedia events and performances that make use of space in more creative ways. The transformation also incorporates sustainability considerations through adaptive reuse, retaining key elements of the former Orchestra Hall while introducing new infrastructure and building systems to improve functionality and operational efficiency. 
This flexibility allows the space to evolve with the needs of its users, providing a future-ready environment that can adapt to changing approaches to how students learn, collaborate and present music as part of their education. 
“As music education evolves, we need spaces that allow students to move beyond fixed performance formats and encourage students to rethink how music can be created, presented and experienced,” said Professor Peter Tornquist, Dean of YST. 
“The Cube brings these possibilities together under one roof, giving students the freedom and flexibility to experiment with new ways of learning, collaborating and performing, while preparing them to navigate and shape the future of music.” 
Creating opportunities for applied learning 
The Cube will provide students with opportunities to apply their learning in a practical environment that mirrors real-world artistic practice. The venue features state-of-the-art audio, visual and lighting systems that brings professional production capabilities that is on par with world-class venues into the student learning environment. 
The Cube’s variable acoustic system allows the room’s acoustic response to be adjusted to suit different uses, while its lighting and multi-projection systems give artists greater flexibility in how performers and audiences are positioned within the space. 
For students, these capabilities provide hands-on opportunities to work with different acoustic conditions, technical setups, spatial configurations and modes of presentation, helping them understand how these choices can shape an artistic outcome. This supports YST’s continued development of its curriculum, including areas that place greater emphasis on student-led performance projects and collaborative music-making. 
“Applied learning is central to the YST experience,” shared YST Assistant Professor Jonathan Shin. 
“The Cube allows for different modes of learning—it gives students a playground to dream in, a laboratory to try practical and creative ways to bring their dreams to life, and a space to learn through the process.” 
The launch of the Cube at Performers(’) Present will demonstrate the versatility of the new venue, with the symposium making use of both the main space and its adjoining pre-function area. Designed as an extension of the Cube, the pre-function area can operate independently as an intimate event space for smaller audiences. 
By hosting activities of this nature within YST, the Cube brings professional artistic and research practices directly into the student learning environment, creating opportunities for students to encounter and engage with different approaches to artistic practice as part of their education. 
Supporting the arts ecosystem at NUS and in Singapore 
The addition of the Cube creates a new focal point for artistic activity within NUS, strengthening the University’s Arts for All (AFA) framework by bringing students across different faculties and disciplines together through the arts. 
“The arts is a deeply fascinating and enriching discipline, and we want every student, whatever their discipline may be, to discover and learn about the arts,” said Professor Tan. 
“They stretch our imagination, give us new lenses to see the world, and deepen our understanding of the human experience.” 
Beyond NUS, the Cube will provide Singapore’s arts community with a new purpose-built platform for performances, rehearsals, creative residencies and collaborative projects. The venue will welcome arts organisations and external hirers, fostering artistic exchange and partnerships between YST and the local arts sector. 
The Cube joins YST’s existing Concert Hall and Recital Studio, expanding the spaces available at the Conservatory to support different scales and forms of artistic activity. Together, these venues reflect YST’s commitment to shaping the future of music education, strengthening connections between students and the professional arts sector while contributing to the cultural landscape of NUS and beyond.

Oxford Battery Modelling Symposium (OBMS) 2027
Location
Mathematical Institute, Oxford, OX2 6GG
Date & Time
Monday 12 Apr 2027 - Tuesday 13 Apr 2027
Availability
The Oxford Battery Modelling Symposium (OBMS) is a unique event for the battery community. OBMS brings together mathematicians, chemists, physicists and engineers from academia and industry to discuss the latest modelling research and applications. Our philosophy is to invite a small number of outstanding speakers spanning a range of topics from atomistic to continuum modelling, controls and beyond, giving broad and inspiring presentations and open discussions. Our first event in 2019 was attended by 170 people with leading experts including John Newman speaking; our subsequent events were held online during lockdown periods but continued to be wildly popular.
The Oxford Battery Modelling Symposium 2027 will be held in the heart of Oxford at the Mathematical Institute.
