title: In the AI Era, Entrepreneurship Educators Seek to Challenge and Motivate Student Founders
summary: Stanford’s Steve Blank, Riitta Katila, and Perry Klebahn encourage educators around the globe to rethink course structure and experiment with new ways to teach the art of innovation
text:
In the AI Era, Entrepreneurship Educators Seek to Challenge and Motivate Student Founders
In the AI age, entrepreneurship educators are having a startup experience, Stanford adjunct professor Perry Klebahn told an international group of educators at an Oct. 13 webinar hosted by the Stanford Technology Ventures Program (STVP).
Like any startup experience, it’s full of uncertainty and chaos.
Klebahn joined Steve Blank, an adjunct professor in the Department of Management Science & Engineering (MS&E), and Riitta Katila, the W. M. Keck Sr. Professor of Management Science and STVP Faculty Director, to discuss how they integrate AI tools as they teach, motivate, and evaluate entrepreneurship students.
“We are going to innovate and change and come out far stronger for that,” said Klebahn, who is director of executive education at the Stanford d.school. “The magic still has to happen. You still have to churn through it. I think you can do it with these tools – I don’t think they need to be excluded.”
With the venture creation processes changing rapidly, the Stanford instructors wanted “to give our colleagues around the world a glimpse of what we are observing here and how the curriculum is really evolving and adapting in real time,” said MS&E Professor and STVP Faculty Director Saikat Chaudhuri, who moderated the panel.
Observations in Stanford’s Startup Courses
In Klebahn and Blank’s courses, AI is reshaping how students begin their startups.
In Klebahn’s LaunchPad (DESIGN 399), student founders launch a company in a quarter. Klebahn previously looked for applicants with a tendency to build. But with AI tools making prototyping dramatically easier, the area of focus has shifted.
Now, founders get stuck refining prototypes instead of “the problem validation and the problem-finding that entrepreneurs naturally did by, frankly, completely missing and then having to go back and toil and work pretty hard to build something,” Klebahn said.
Blank has seen a similar pattern in Lean LaunchPad (ENGR 245), where student teams test startup ideas with customers. For years, Blank’s students started with customer interviews and a minimum viable product. This year, every team already had a digital twin or demo ready.
“We had to pry what they thought was a finished product out of their hands and get them to actually spend time trying to deeply understand customer problems and needs,” he said.
Blank’s teaching team decided to “rejigger the entire class,” which Blank documented on his blog. Now, students dive into customer discovery and must work with a design partner. Instead of an MVP, they refer to their IUP: “initial untested product.”
Embracing the Human Connection
The challenges presented by AI aren’t limited to entrepreneurs in the classroom.
Katila co-authored a forthcoming paper in Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal examining how early-stage entrepreneurs around the world are adapting to AI. She found that “expertise is being decoupled from the production, the struggle, the suffering of creating something.”
Educators need to motivate students to think about the reasoning behind their work, she said. “How do we get our students to become experts in a world where everything is – everywhere, all at once – at your fingertips?”
The panelists emphasized the importance of integrating human connection alongside AI tools.
Blank expects his students to use AI to accelerate getting products to customers.
“I think it will be a while before AI is buying from AI,” he said. “As long as human beings are involved, then it’s people who have the problems.”
At a recent meeting with Stanford first-year students, Katila was intrigued to learn their appreciation for small-group discussions. She suggested bringing in more course assistants for conversations.
Klebahn has been studying critique techniques and looking for ways to teach self-awareness and discernment. This is additionally challenging because more students are now working solo rather than in teams.
“If you want to work alone, that’s amazing,” he said. “I still want to land that there is enormous value to being vulnerable and showing this to other people.”
A group of alumni who guest-taught LaunchPad recently had the students switch projects with each other.
“I could see the lights go on for so many students: ‘Oh I never thought of all these decisions I’ve made that now somebody else is exposing by working on my stuff,’” Klebahn said.
Practical Advice for Educators
Blank urged entrepreneurship educators to understand that everything they taught last year is now obsolete.
It helps to go back to first principles, he said: Figure out what you truly want students to learn and consider how to use AI to prepare them for the world – “not the world that we wish they lived in, but the world that they’re going to live in.”
Katila and Klebahn said educators should see teaching in the time of AI as an exciting opportunity, and Klebahn encouraged them to be transparent about the need to experiment.
“You’re going to live a lifetime with these tools, and you’re at an unbelievable point to be involved with smart co-founders and founders in the classroom and good professors, and we are asking these questions together,” he envisioned telling students. “It’s a fabulous experience to learn about this.”
